name: Auditing Smart Contracts
title: Auditing Smart Contracts
answer: Auditing smart contracts is the practice of reviewing the code, state transitions, and economic logic of programs that execute on a blockchain. The work focuses on whether a contract correctly handles asset custody, transfers, access control, and edge cases such as reentrancy or arithmetic errors. In digital asset accounting, this review supports the reliability of balances, transaction records, and automated financial obligations recorded on chain. An audit typically covers both the source code and the deployed bytecode, along with the parameters and upgrade paths that affect future behavior.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Auditing smart contracts is the practice of reviewing the code, state transitions, and economic logic of programs that execute on a blockchain. The work focuses on whether a contract correctly handles asset custody, transfers, access control, and edge cases such as reentrancy or arithmetic errors. In digital asset accounting, this review supports the reliability of balances, transaction records, and automated financial obligations recorded on chain. An audit typically covers both the source code and the deployed bytecode, along with the parameters and upgrade paths that affect future behavior.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on local development environments that fork a blockchain's state, on public test networks, and against live mainnet data where read only access is needed. Auditors use static analysis tools, symbolic execution engines, fuzz testing frameworks, and formal verification assistants to exercise contract paths. Node access and block explorers provide the transaction history and storage layout needed to compare intended behavior with actual state changes. Some reviews also run in containerized environments that reproduce compiler versions and dependency builds.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: An audit usually begins with a specification review to establish what the contract is supposed to do, followed by line by line manual inspection of the code. Automated tools then scan for known vulnerability patterns, while fuzzing and symbolic execution generate unusual inputs and explore state space. Auditors test invariants such as total supply conservation, collateral ratios, and access control boundaries, and they simulate attacks like reentrancy, front running, and oracle manipulation. The final step compares the audited source code to the bytecode deployed at a specific address and documents any differences or unresolved findings.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Audit reports are point in time opinions, not guarantees, and they typically state the exact commit hash, deployment address, and scope of files reviewed. Users and protocol teams rely on these reports to allocate risk, but liability for losses often remains with the deploying team and users rather than the auditor. Provenance matters because a contract may be upgradeable or controlled by a multisig, so the audited code can change after the report is issued. Best practice includes publishing the audit scope, linking the report to the deployed bytecode, and maintaining a bug bounty or incident response process for later discoveries.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous monitoring of deployed contracts rather than one time pre launch reviews. Formal verification and AI assisted code review are becoming more common for high value protocols, especially where accounting invariants must hold across many interacting contracts. Standardized audit checklists and machine readable findings are likely to support automated re-audits when dependencies or governance parameters change. Cross chain bridges and modular upgrade patterns will push auditors to track provenance and risk across multiple networks and execution environments.
